chunks.text: 2 Method We propose LowBridge, a framework for cross-modal medical image segmentation, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . There is a source labeled dataset, I s = { x i s , y i s } i = 1 N s I^{s}=\left\{{x_{i}^{s},y_{i}^{s}}\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}} , consisting of N s N_{s} pairs of labeled images and their corresponding labels, where each image, x i s ∈ ℝ H × W x_{i}^{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} , and its label, y i s ∈ ℝ n × H × W y_{i}^{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times H\times W} , have a height H H , width W W and n n classes. At deployment, LowBridge is applied to an unseen target-domain unlabeled dataset, I t = { x i t } i = 1 N t I^{t}=\left\{{x_{i}^{t}}\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{t}} , acquired from a different modality ( e.g. MRI vs. CT) but imaging the same anatomical region ( e.g. abdomen). Our goal is to train a generative model, 𝒢 ⁡ ( ⋅ , β g ​ e ​ n ) \mathcal{G}(\cdot;\beta_{gen}) , parameterized by β g ​ e ​ n \beta_{gen} , and a segmentation model, 𝒮 ⁡ ( ⋅ , β s ​ e ​ g ) \mathcal{S}(\cdot;\beta_{seg}) , parameterized by β s ​ e ​ g \beta_{seg} , using the source labeled dataset, I s I^{s} . The trained models will then be applied to the target unlabeled dataset I t I^{t} for cross-modal segmentation. 2.1 Training on the source domain For source-only cross-modal DG, the objective is to learn source-domain representations that remain informative when applied to an unseen target modality. In this work, we exploit the observation that low-level features, namely edges, in medical images are relatively invariant to domain shift, making them a reliable foundation for aligning the target domain distribution with the source domain distribution for cross-modal image segmentation. Edge feature extraction.

We first employ an off-the-shelf edge detector ℰ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{E}(\cdot) on the source domain images, { x i s } i = 1 N s \left\{{x_{i}^{s}}\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}} to extract their corresponding edge features { e i s } i = 1 N s \left\{{e_{i}^{s}}\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}} , where e i s ∈ ℝ H × W e^{s}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} provides an outline of the anatomical structures present in the image. This process is denoted as: e i s = ℰ ⁡ ( x i s ) . \displaystyle e^{s}_{i}=\mathcal{E}(x^{s}_{i}). (1) Following evaluation of various edge detection algorithms, we selected the Canny detector [ 16 ] as our default edge detector, given its excellent noise immunity, multi-scale, and high-precision detection capabilities. Edge-to-image reconstruction. Next, we train a generative model, 𝒢 ⁡ ( ⋅ , β g ​ e ​ n ) \mathcal{G}(\cdot;\beta_{gen}) , to reconstruct the source domain images from their corresponding edge features, e i s e^{s}_{i} . This process can be expressed as: g i s = 𝒢 ⁡ ( e i s , β g ​ e ​ n ) , \displaystyle g^{s}_{i}=\mathcal{G}(e^{s}_{i};\beta_{gen}), (2) where g i s ∈ ℝ H × W g^{s}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} represents the generated source image, which aims to replicate the original source domain image x i s x^{s}_{i} . The generative model 𝒢 ⁡ ( ⋅ , β g ​ e ​ n ) \mathcal{G}(\cdot;\beta_{gen}) is trained using the mean squared error ℒ M ​ S ​ E \mathcal{L}_{MSE} as the loss function, denoted as: ℒ g ​ e ​ n = ℒ M ​ S ​ E ​ ( g i s , x i s ) . \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{gen}=\mathcal{L}_{MSE}(g^{s}_{i},x^{s}_{i}). (3) We investigate several generator architectures, including encoder-decoder architecture ( e.g. [ 17 ] ) and adversarial architecture ( e.g. [ 18 ] ), within the proposed framework in Sec. 3.3 . Segmentation.

Finally, we train a segmentation model 𝒮 ⁡ ( ⋅ , β s ​ e ​ g ) \mathcal{S}(\cdot;\beta_{seg}) using the reconstructed source images, { g i s } i = 1 N s \left\{{g_{i}^{s}}\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}} , and their corresponding labels, { y i s } i = 1 N s \left\{{y_{i}^{s}}\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}} . The segmentation predictions, { p i s } i = 1 N s \left\{{p_{i}^{s}}\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}} , are obtained through: p i s = 𝒮 ⁡ ( g i s , β s ​ e ​ g ) . \displaystyle p^{s}_{i}=\mathcal{S}(g^{s}_{i};\beta_{seg}). (4) To optimize the segmentation model, we define the segmentation loss, ℒ s ​ e ​ g \mathcal{L}_{seg} , as a combination of the cross-entropy loss, ℒ C ​ E \mathcal{L}_{CE} , and the Dice loss, ℒ D ​ i ​ c ​ e \mathcal{L}_{Dice} : ℒ S ​ e ​ g = α c ​ e ​ ℒ C ​ E ​ ( p i s , y i s ) + α d ​ i ​ c ​ e ​ ℒ D ​ i ​ c ​ e ​ ( p i s , y i s ) , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Seg}=\alpha_{ce}\mathcal{L}_{CE}(p^{s}_{i},y^{s}_{i})+\alpha_{dice}\mathcal{L}_{Dice}(p^{s}_{i},y^{s}_{i}), (5) where α c ​ e \alpha_{ce} and α d ​ i ​ c ​ e \alpha_{dice} are the weights of the respective losses. In our experiments in Sec. 3.3 , we instantiate the segmentation model, 𝒮 ⁡ ( ⋅ , β s ​ e ​ g ) \mathcal{S}(\cdot;\beta_{seg}) , with several tested architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [ 19 ] , Transformers [ 17 ] , and hybrid models. 2.2 Segmentation on the target domain At test time, we utilize the trained models from Sec. 2.1 to segment unlabeled cross-modal target domain images, I t = { x i t } i = 1 N t I^{t}=\left\{{x_{i}^{t}}\right\}_{i=1}^{N_{t}} . Specifically, we first extract the edge feature, e i t e^{t}_{i} , from x i t x_{i}^{t} using the same edge detector ℰ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{E}(\cdot) employed in Eq. ( 1 ), ensuring structural consistency between target and source domain edge representations.

The edge feature e i t e^{t}_{i} is then input into the pretrained generator, 𝒢 ⁡ ( ⋅ , β g ​ e ​ n ) \mathcal{G}(\cdot;\beta_{gen}) , to synthesize a source-style target image, g i t g^{t}_{i} , as described in Eq. ( 2 ). By exploiting modality-shared edge information, g i t g^{t}_{i} inherits structural details from x i t x^{t}_{i} while adopting the appearance traits from the source domain, thereby bridging the domain gap. Finally, the source-style target image g i t g^{t}_{i} is segmented using the trained segmentation model, 𝒮 ⁡ ( ⋅ , β s ​ e ​ g ) \mathcal{S}(\cdot;\beta_{seg}) , as outlined in Eq. ( 4 ). Notably, the entire inference process does not require fine-tuning on target domain data, maintaining complete test-time efficiency. 3 Experiments and Results 3.1 Experimental Setup To evaluate the proposed LowBridge, we conducted cross-modal segmentation experiments ( i.e. , MRI → \rightarrow CT and CT → \rightarrow MRI) for liver and cardiac substructure segmentation on two publicly available datasets. Here, → \rightarrow denotes knowledge transfer between modalities. Datasets. For liver segmentation, we employed the CHAOS dataset [ 20 ] from ISBI 2019 CHAOS Challenge, which contains 20 sets of three-sequence MRI ( i.e. , T1 In-phase, T1 Out-phase, and T2) and CT images, with pixel-level liver annotations. The voxel spacing is 1.36 × 1.89 × ( 5.5 ∼ 9.0 ) ​ m ​ m 3 1.36\times 1.89\times(5.5\sim 9.0)mm^{3} for MRI and 0.7 × 0.8 × ( 3.0 ∼ 3.2 ) ​ m ​ m 3 0.7\times 0.8\times(3.0\sim 3.2)mm^{3} for CT. For simplicity and proof of concept, we used only the T1 In-phase sequence as the MRI modality. For cardiac substructure segmentation, we utilized the MMWHS 2017 dataset [ 21 ] , which includes 20 unpaired MRI and CT volumetric scans, with voxel spacings of 2 × 2 × 2 ​ m ​ m 3 2\times 2\times 2mm^{3} and 0.44 × 0.44 × 0.60 ​ m ​ m 3 0.44\times 0.44\times 0.60mm^{3} , respectively.

] , SE-ASA [ 10 ] , MA-UDA [ 8 ] , and TCSA [ 23 ] . Our LowBridge operates in a more restrictive source-only setting ( i.e. without access to target-domain samples during training) than the UDA baselines ( i.e. with access to target-domain images during training). Therefore, the comparison provides a challenging reference setting for LowBridge. The results of each method were obtained from the corresponding paper or running the released code. Liver Segmentation. As shown in Table 1 and Fig. 2 , our LowBridge outperformed ten existing SOTA methods. Compared with the top-performing MPSCL [ 11 ] , LowBridge achieved improvements of 3.8 % \% in Dice and 11.4 % \% in ASD, respectively. Cardiac Substructure Segmentation. Table 2 and Fig. 2 demonstrate the SOTA performance of LowBridge. Specifically, LowBridge surpassed MPSCL [ 11 ] by 4.9 % \% in average Dice and 12.3 % \% in average ASD. Although slightly lower performance was observed for some structures, such as LVC in MR → \rightarrow CT and LAC in CT → \rightarrow MR, LowBridge still outperformed existing UDA methods overall. These performance drops may reflect limitations of hand-crafted edge extraction in low-contrast or heterogeneous regions, which should be addressed in future work. Notably, LowBridge outperforms UDA baselines despite having no access to target-domain samples during training. This highlights LowBridge’s potential for clinical applications, where target-modality data may not always be available before deployment. 3.3 Ablation Studies To assess the architectural sensitivity of LowBridge, we evaluated various generative and segmentation models on the CHAOS dataset. As shown in Table 3 , the four segmenters achieved comparable performance, with average absolute deviations of 0.38 in Dice and 1.19 in ASD. Despite these variations, they outperformed most existing methods in Table 1 . Generative models . We investigated different generative models for LowBridge, including GAN [ 18 ] (with a pretrained ResNet-50 [ 27 ] encoder), DDPM [ 28 ] , SwinUNet [ 17 ] , and FreUNet, with UNet [ 19 ] as the segmentation model. As shown in Table 3 , the four generators yielded varying performance, with an average PSNR gap of 6.08 between the best and worst models. Overall, higher generation quality was associated with better final performance. Edge-only segmentation. Training the segmenter directly on edge maps (row 8, Table 3 ) yielded substantially lower performance, highlighting the importance of image reconstruction for LowBridge. Inference speed. On an NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU, the standalone generative ( i.e. FreUNet) and segmentation ( i.e. SwinUNet) models process 43.6 and 67.1 slices per second, respectively, with negligible Canny latency. Despite multi‑stage sequential overhead, LowBridge maintains practical inference efficiency for clinical use. Limitations and future work.

Our ablation studies demonstrate that LowBridge is compatible with various tested generative and segmentation architectures. While different segmenters achieved comparable or better performance than most existing methods in Table 1 , the relatively poor performance of GAN and DDPM suggests that the primary bottleneck of LowBridge’s performance lies in the capability of the generative model to reconstruct high-quality images from their low-level edge features. Moreover, this work primarily exploits hand‑crafted Canny edges as low-level features for MRI-CT segmentation. Future endeavour may continue the investigation on the robustness of other low-level features for more general cross-modality medical image segmentation. 4 Conclusion In this paper, we proposed LowBridge, a source-only DG framework for cross-modal medical image segmentation. By treating low-level edge features as domain-invariant representations, we designed a simple yet effective strategy to reconstruct source-style target-domain images for segmentation. Extensive experiments on two publicly available MRI-CT benchmark datasets demonstrated that LowBridge achieves SOTA performance, surpassing ten existing methods without access to target-domain samples during training. Moreover, ablation studies confirmed its flexibility and compatibility with various generative and segmentation models, highlighting its potential for further improvement with more advanced techniques. This work opens up new possibilities for effective cross-modal generalization in medical image segmentation, paving the way for more robust and generalizable solutions in clinical applications.
